SUPREME COURT OF INDIA · CHILDREN ONLINE Protect children online. Don't push them offline. On 15 October 2026, the Supreme Court held that internet access is a fundamental right for children too, rejected blanket bans, and ordered platforms to take on more of the work of protecting them. THE CASE Just Rights for Children Alliance v. S. Harish ORDER DATED BENCH 15 Oct 2026 Pardiwala & A detailed order of about 136 Chandran, JJ. pages Supreme Court of India BACKGROUND Follow-up to the 2024 CSEAM judgment An NGO told the Court that platforms were still failing to remove child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) two years after the 23 Sept 2024 judgment. NEXT HEARING 10 December 2026 The Centre must file an affidavit on compliance progress before then. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 02 / 08

A right, not a risk to be banned “To keep the child away from the internet on account of such failures would be to mistake the victim for the problem.” 1 Internet access is a fundamental right of every individual, children included, under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a). 2 Blanket bans are disproportionate. They may push children to unregulated platforms and stop them reporting abuse. 3 Checking every user's age carries its own risk of sensitive data collection and surveillance. 4 Platforms that ignore POCSO and IT Rules duties cannot rely on safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. Where this meets Section 9 of the DPDP Act DPDP ACT, S. 9 Verifiable parental consent Required before processing data of anyone under 18. No tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted ads aimed at children. Applies from 13 May 2027. THE TENSION Consent needs age checks; the Court warns about them The Court cautioned that checking every user's age risks collecting sensitive data. Platforms must verify consent in a way that collects as little data as possible. FOR PLATFORMS & ED-TECH Design "child mode" now Private defaults, no profiling of children, light-touch age assurance, and a grievance system ready for 24-hour acknowledgements. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 07 / 08

TA K E AWAY The burden shifts from children to platforms. Instead of keeping children offline, the Court has made platforms responsible for detecting, removing and reporting abuse. Between this order and the DPDP Act, child safety is now a legal design requirement. Adv.
